stories.headline: Sensex jumps 2% as AI-heavy Korea and Japan fall 6%
stories.question: Why are Indian stocks rising while Asia's AI-heavy markets crash after the US midterms?
stories.dek: Fears of a US backlash against AI hit tech-heavy markets in Korea and Japan hardest. Foreign investors kept buying Indian shares, lifting the Sensex for a seventh straight session and strengthening the rupee.

so_far.text: On 5 November 2026, after the US midterm elections, AI and chip stocks crashed. The Nasdaq, a US index heavy with tech firms, fell 5.5% to 24,315, and the Dow fell 3.4%. Reports linked the fall to fears that Democratic gains could slow the building of data centres, the huge computer buildings that run AI. Senator Bernie Sanders has called for a national moratorium, or pause, on data-centre construction.

what_happened.text: On 6 November the selloff spread to Asia. South Korea's Kospi closed down 6.0% at 5,059.69, and Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 6.0% to 57,434.77. Nikkei Asia said tech shares in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan took the most pressure. India moved the other way. The Sensex rose 1,718.01 points, or 2.17%, to 81,028.02. The Nifty rose 493.75 points to 25,030.35, a nine-month high. The rupee strengthened past 94 per dollar. Foreign institutional investors had bought ₹14,974.68 crore of Indian shares on 5 November.

steps.text: Democratic midterm gains raised fears that US data-centre building could slow, putting pressure on the AI spending boom.
Investors sold the firms that profit most from that boom: chip-makers and AI cloud firms like CoreWeave, which fell 10%.

India's rally leaned on bank shares, not chip-makers, and foreign investors kept buying Indian shares.

lesson.concept: How an index's mix decides its move
lesson.big_idea: A stock index is a weighted basket of companies. A shock to one industry hits hardest the markets where that industry is a big part of the basket.

steps.title: An index is a basket
steps.text: A stock index, like India's Sensex or Korea's Kospi, is one number that tracks a basket of big companies. When most prices in the basket rise, the index rises.

steps.title: Each group has a weight
steps.text: Bigger companies count for more. A group's weight is its share of the basket's total value. If chip-makers are half the basket's value, their weight is 50%.

steps.title: Weight times move, then add
steps.text: Each group's contribution is its weight multiplied by its price move that day. Add every group's contribution together and you get the index's move.

steps.title: Money moves between baskets
steps.text: When investors sell one theme, they can buy elsewhere. Foreign institutional investors, meaning overseas funds, bought ₹14,974.68 crore of Indian shares on 5 November. Their buying pushes up prices, and the rupee.

example.setup: Imagine two made-up markets, A and B. In one day, chip shares everywhere fall 12%. Assume chips are half of Market A, but only a tenth of Market B.

lines.label: Market A: chip drag
lines.note: Half the basket is chips (assumed).

lines.label: Market A: the rest
lines.note: Assume everything else stays flat.

lines.label: Market A total
lines.note: The chip crash sets the whole day.

lines.label: Market B: chip drag
lines.note: Same crash, much smaller weight.

lines.label: Market B: banks and others
lines.note: Assume foreign buying lifts banks and other shares.

lines.label: Market B total
lines.note: The gains outweigh the chip drag.

example.result: The same chip crash knocks Market A down 6% but leaves Market B up 0.6%. What a market holds decides how much a global shock hurts it.

apply.text: This is close to what happened on 6 November. Nikkei Asia said tech shares in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan took the most pressure, and the Kospi and Nikkei fell 6.0%. In India, Business Standard linked the rally to rising bank shares as the global AI trade unwound. Foreign buying added a push, and the Sensex rose 2.17%.

practice.q: Imagine Market C, where chips are 30% of the index. Chips fall 10% and everything else rises 1%. How does Market C move?
practice.answer: Chip drag: 30% × −10% = −3%. The rest: 70% × +1% = +0.7%. Total: −3% + 0.7% = −2.3%. Market C falls 2.3%, between Market A and Market B.

stories.headline: After Ueno Bank collapse, Paraguay's lower house impeaches President Peña
stories.question: How did one bank's collapse push Paraguay's president toward the exit within days?
stories.dek: Ueno Bank's books hid how thin its safety cushion was. Its failure cut off about 3 million customers and trapped public funds. Lawmakers accuse President Peña of a conflict of interest.

so_far.text: Ueno Bank is a digital lender in Paraguay, a country of about 6.5 million people. In under five years it grew from an obscure finance company into a household name. It claimed over 60% of adults as customers. It also held public money, including the state pension and health fund. President Santiago Peña appointed Carlos Carvallo, who had led Ueno's predecessor, to head the central bank that supervised Ueno. Peña reportedly held a stake in Ueno's holding company until 2025. In June 2026 inspectors flagged risky insider lending. In October 2026 Peña still called the warnings a smear campaign.

what_happened.text: Paraguay's central bank seized Ueno Bank. Regulators found poorly documented loans to companies tied to its owners, and expenses counted as assets. After correction, its capital fell below half the legal minimum. Ueno's app, cards and transfers went offline. Eight senior executives, including founder Miguel Vázquez, were detained, and 27 officials and associates were charged. Importers and retailers warned that sales at major retailers could fall by 35%. On 5 November 2026 Peña tried to resign. Colorado Party lawmakers walked out, Congress lost quorum, and the resignation was not accepted. The lower house voted 78–0 to impeach him. The Senate summoned him to appear on 6 November.

steps.text: Ueno lent large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond legal limits and with weak collateral.
It also counted expenses as assets, so its safety cushion looked bigger than it really was.
Once the books were corrected, capital fell below half the legal minimum, and the central bank seized Ueno.
About 3 million customers and $800–850 million of public money were suddenly caught inside a failed bank.
Lawmakers alleged a conflict of interest over Peña's links to Ueno. Cartes withdrew support, citing "theft of public, private and pension funds".

lesson.concept: How a bank's capital cushion protects depositors
lesson.big_idea: A bank's capital is its safety cushion: what it owns minus what it owes depositors. If the owned side is padded with fake or shaky assets, the cushion is thinner than it looks.

steps.title: Deposits are what a bank owes
steps.text: A bank takes your deposits and lends most of them out. The loans are its assets, what it owns. The deposits are its debts, what it must repay.

steps.title: Capital is the gap
steps.text: Capital is assets minus debts. It is the owners' own money in the bank. When a loan goes bad, this cushion absorbs the loss first.

steps.title: The law sets a minimum
steps.text: Regulators demand a minimum cushion. If capital falls far below it, they can seize the bank. Ueno's corrected capital was under half the legal minimum.

steps.title: Fake assets make it look thick
steps.text: Counting spending as an asset, or lending to owners' firms with weak collateral, makes capital look bigger than it is. Regulators found both at Ueno.

example.setup: Imagine a small bank that reports ₹110 crore of assets, mostly loans, and owes ₹100 crore to depositors. Assume the law demands at least ₹10 crore of capital.

lines.label: Reported capital
lines.note: Exactly at the assumed minimum, so it looks fine.

lines.label: Remove booked spending
lines.note: Assume ₹2 crore of spending was listed as assets.

lines.label: Write off insider loans
lines.note: Assume ₹4 crore lent to owners' firms on weak collateral won't return.

lines.label: Compare with minimum
lines.calc: Half of ₹10 crore = ₹5 crore; ₹4 crore is less
lines.note: Below half the minimum, like Ueno after correction.

lines.label: Cushion per ₹100 deposited
lines.note: Any further loss quickly reaches depositors' money.

example.result: No cash left the bank. Only honest accounting changed. A cushion that looked like ₹10 crore was really ₹4 crore, below half the minimum, which is when a regulator steps in.

apply.text: That is what happened at Ueno. Regulators stripped out expenses counted as assets and examined poorly documented loans to owners' companies, including nearly $39 million in one day in September 2025. Capital fell below half the legal minimum, so the central bank seized Ueno. With 3 million customers and $800–850 million of public money inside, the failure became political.

practice.q: Same bank, but no spending was hidden and only ₹1 crore of insider loans must be written off. Is it below half the minimum?
practice.answer: Start at ₹10 crore of capital. Subtract ₹1 crore: ₹9 crore. Half the ₹10 crore minimum is ₹5 crore. ₹9 crore is above that, so no. It is still ₹1 crore short of the full minimum, so the owners would need to add capital.

check.why: Capital is assets minus what the bank owes. Removing fake assets shrinks capital directly, before any money leaves the bank.

takeaways: A bank's capital is what it owns minus what it owes; losses hit it first.

lesson.concept: How divided government limits a US president
lesson.big_idea: When the other party controls Congress, the president cannot pass new laws alone, and Congress cannot easily beat his veto. Each side blocks the other, so the White House leans on executive action.

steps.title: Laws need both chambers
steps.text: A bill becomes law only if a majority in the House and a majority in the Senate pass it. The House has 435 seats, so 218 is a majority. The president then signs the bill or vetoes it, meaning rejects it.

steps.title: Beating a veto needs two-thirds
steps.text: Congress can still turn a vetoed bill into law. But two-thirds of both chambers must vote for it again. That is 290 of 435 House members and 67 of 100 senators.

steps.title: A majority can block, not command
steps.text: A simple majority can stop the president's bills and refuse money for his plans. It usually cannot force its own bills through, because majorities rarely reach two-thirds.

steps.title: Oversight is the other tool
steps.text: The majority chairs every committee. Chairs can issue subpoenas, legal orders to testify or hand over papers, and hold hearings into officials. The House can impeach; removal needs two-thirds of the Senate.

steps.title: The president turns to his staff
steps.text: Blocked in Congress, a president relies more on executive orders and agencies he already controls. The chief of staff, who needs no Senate approval, runs that machine day to day.

stories.headline: Very strong El Niño puts 2027 on track for record heat
stories.question: What does a very strong El Niño mean for global heat and India's weather next year?
stories.dek: The warm Pacific heats the air with a delay, so 2027 looks likely to be the hottest year on record. For India, a warmer winter and harsher heat are possible.

so_far.text: El Niño is a natural swing in the Pacific Ocean. Every few years, the surface of the central and eastern Pacific turns warmer than usual. That shifts rain and heat around the world. The planet is also warming because of greenhouse gases. Copernicus, the EU climate service, says August 2026 was the joint hottest month on record. In October 2026, NOAA's Climate Prediction Center said a strong-to-very-strong El Niño was likely through January–March 2027. It put the chance at more than 83%.

what_happened.text: On 5 November 2026, Grist reported that the current El Niño is already the strongest on record. It said the El Niño could strengthen further in the coming months. NOAA's outlook for December 2026 to February 2027 favours a wetter winter from California to the Carolinas. On 6 November, climate scientists quoted by DW said the world is set to breach 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels in 2026. Carbon Brief projects 2027 near 1.7°C, with a 96% chance of being the warmest year on record.

steps.text: Normally, steady winds push warm surface water west across the Pacific, and cold water rises in the east.
In an El Niño, those winds weaken, so a huge sheet of warm water spreads east across the surface.
That warm sea surface hands heat to the air above, lifting the world's average temperature.
The air warms months after the ocean peaks, so the following year usually gets the biggest boost.
The boost sits on top of human-caused warming, which is why records came in 1998, 2016 and 2024.

lesson.concept: Why El Niño heat shows up the next year
lesson.big_idea: El Niño moves Pacific heat from the ocean into the air. The air warms months after the ocean peaks, so the year after a big El Niño usually gets the biggest boost.

steps.title: A normal Pacific
steps.text: Usually, steady winds blow warm surface water west, towards Asia. Cold water rises from the deep near South America. That keeps a large part of the Pacific surface cool.

steps.title: El Niño flips it
steps.text: When those winds weaken, warm water spreads east across the surface. NOAA grades strength by how much warmer than normal the water runs. 'Very strong' means at least +2°C for three months.

steps.title: The ocean heats the air
steps.text: A warm sea surface gives off heat and moisture to the air above it. Across an ocean area this big, that lifts the whole planet's average temperature.

steps.title: The air lags behind
steps.text: Air temperature catches up slowly, a few months after the ocean peaks. So an El Niño that peaks late in one year warms the next year most. Record years followed big El Niños in 1998, 2016 and 2024.

steps.title: Stacked on the trend
steps.text: The El Niño boost adds to long-term warming from greenhouse gases. So each new El Niño starts from a higher base than the last one did.

example.setup: Imagine long-term warming puts a normal year at 1.4°C above pre-industrial. A big El Niño peaks in December of Year 1. Assume it adds 0.05°C to Year 1 and 0.2°C to Year 2.

lines.label: Normal year
lines.note: Background warming from greenhouse gases

lines.label: Year 1 total
lines.note: Only the last few months feel the El Niño

lines.label: Year 2 total
lines.note: The air has caught up, so the whole year feels it

lines.label: Gap between years
lines.note: Same El Niño, bigger effect the year after

example.result: The same El Niño adds four times more heat to Year 2 than to Year 1. The heat shows up in the air after the ocean has already peaked.

apply.text: This is the pattern forecasters see now. Carbon Brief puts January–September 2026 at about 1.45°C above pre-industrial, behind only 2024. NOAA expects a strong El Niño through January–March 2027. Carbon Brief projects 2027 near 1.7°C, with a 96% chance of being the warmest year on record.

practice.q: Suppose a normal year is 1.5°C and an El Niño adds 0.1°C in Year 1 and 0.25°C in Year 2. Which year is hotter, and by how much?
practice.answer: Year 1: 1.5 + 0.1 = 1.6°C. Year 2: 1.5 + 0.25 = 1.75°C. Gap: 1.75 − 1.6 = 0.15°C. Year 2 is hotter, because the air keeps warming after the ocean peaks.

stories.headline: UPI shop fee: NPCI tells Supreme Court customers won't pay
stories.question: Will paying shops by UPI soon cost money, and who will actually pay?
stories.dek: Not you at the counter. NPCI told the Supreme Court that shops must absorb a planned fee of up to 0.4% on UPI payments above ₹2,000. Apps cannot add charges either.

so_far.text: UPI lets you pay a shop by scanning a QR code. Until now, shops have paid no fee to accept it. A revised framework allows a fee, called MDR, of up to 0.4% on payments to shops above ₹2,000. It was due to start on 15 October, but NPCI, which runs UPI, postponed it. No new date has been given. Separately, advocate Anjan Datta challenged the fee in the Supreme Court. On 28 September the court refused to pause it. It asked the Centre, RBI and NPCI to respond.

what_happened.text: On 3 November NPCI filed its written reply, called a counter-affidavit, in the Supreme Court. It defended the fee. NPCI told the court that merchants cannot pass the fee on to customers. UPI apps cannot charge a platform fee either. NPCI called this bar binding and enforceable. A payment provider or app that breaks it can lose its UPI membership. NPCI said zero fees left a cost gap that limits spending on infrastructure and security. It said the fee touches only about 4% of merchant UPI payments. Reports on the reply give no new start date.

lesson.concept: How a merchant fee on UPI payments works
lesson.big_idea: When a shop accepts a digital payment, the firms that move the money can take a small cut, called MDR. The shop pays it from what it receives. The customer pays the normal price.

steps.title: Many firms move one payment
steps.text: When you pay a shop by UPI, money moves from your bank to the shop's bank. Apps and NPCI's network carry the instructions. Each firm has costs to run its part.

steps.title: MDR is the shop's fee
steps.text: MDR, the merchant discount rate, is a percentage cut taken from the shop's receipt. The firms in the chain share it. Under the new framework it is capped at 0.4%.

steps.title: Only bigger payments count
steps.text: The fee applies only to person-to-merchant payments above ₹2,000. Smaller payments stay free. NPCI says this hits about 4% of merchant UPI transactions.

steps.title: Your price stays the same
steps.text: NPCI says shops cannot add the fee to your bill, and apps cannot charge a platform fee. A provider that breaks this can lose its UPI membership.

steps.title: A slice helps small shops
steps.text: Each firm puts 5% of its share of the fee into a fund for small merchants. These are shops with turnover up to ₹20 lakh.

practice.q: A shop gets a ₹10,000 UPI payment for a phone. At the full 0.4% fee, what does the shop keep, and what do you pay?
practice.answer: ₹10,000 is above ₹2,000, so the fee applies. 0.4% of ₹10,000 = ₹40. The shop keeps ₹10,000 − ₹40 = ₹9,960. You still pay ₹10,000, because the shop cannot pass the fee on.

sections.title: World
sections.gist: Iran reports more tankers burning near Hormuz, but oil still fell for the week. Trump says a Ukraine deal is near but gives no terms.

items.headline: Iran reports two more tankers hit mines near Hormuz
items.text: On Thursday 5 November, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two more oil tankers struck mines in and near the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire. Iran says five tankers in total have caught fire after hitting naval mines, the South China Morning Post reported. Maritime officials have not confirmed any of these incidents. Brent crude, a global benchmark oil price, fell below $100 a barrel on 4 November for the first time since September, to about $94. On 5 November it rose 2.2% to $96.70 as the market reaction to the US midterm elections faded. CNBC reported oil prices fell over the week. It is not yet known whether the tanker reports will be independently confirmed.
items.background: Iran says oil tankers are striking naval mines in and near the Strait of Hormuz. Outside maritime officials have not confirmed these reports.
items.why: Investors are pricing Iran conflict risk into oil, and Brent swung between about $94 and $96.70 in two days.

items.headline: Trump says Russia–Ukraine deal is near after meeting Putin's envoy
items.text: On 5 November, Donald Trump met Kirill Dmitriev at the White House. Dmitriev is Russian President Vladimir Putin's envoy. Afterwards Trump said a Russia–Ukraine deal is near and spoke of a 'big agreement'. He disclosed no terms. Separately, Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials at the White House. She called for a more lasting truce. Nobody has said what a deal would cover or when it might be signed. Watch for any written terms and for whether Kyiv and Moscow confirm Trump's account.
items.background: US envoy Witkoff's diplomacy has not produced a wider ceasefire. A six-day truce in Kherson ended before 2 November, and Russian strikes continued.
items.why: There is no direct effect on India yet. A real ceasefire would change Europe's largest war, but no terms are known.

sections.title: India
sections.gist: Pralay missile nears induction. Supreme Court rules on OBC creamy layer and UGC equity rules. SIR row grows over fake deletion forms. India signs new energy deals.

items.headline: Pralay missile passes army user trial off Odisha coast
items.text: On 5 November 2026, DRDO, India's defence research agency, flight-tested the Pralay missile from Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island off Odisha. It was a user evaluation trial, a test run for the forces that would use it, and it met all its set objectives. Pralay is a solid-fuel, surface-to-surface missile. Its range is about 150 to 500 km, and it carries a payload of 500 to 1,000 kg. It follows a quasi-ballistic flight path, which makes it harder to intercept than conventional ballistic missiles. The Defence Secretary and the DRDO Chairman said the trial means the missile will join the armed forces soon. No induction date has been given.
items.background: Before a weapon joins the armed forces, it must pass user trials. These tests check it against what the military needs.
items.why: Pralay is moving from development to service, adding a ground-launched missile with a range of up to about 500 km to India's arsenal.

items.headline: Supreme Court refuses to delay its OBC creamy-layer ruling
items.text: On 6 November, the Supreme Court rejected the Centre's request to apply its 11 March ruling only to future cases. The case is Union of India v. Rohith Nathan. In March, the Court said a parent's salary from a PSU or private job cannot by itself put an OBC candidate in the 'creamy layer'. Candidates in the creamy layer are treated as better-off and lose OBC reservation. The Court has now said the March reading must govern how services are allotted to OBC candidates selected through the Civil Services Examination 2025. The Centre had asked for more time, citing 'administrative chaos'. It has not yet said how it will redo the allotments.
items.background: OBC reservation excludes the 'creamy layer', better-off families. How their income is counted decides who qualifies for reserved seats and posts.
items.why: OBC candidates from the 2025 civil services exam who were excluded only on parental salary could now be allotted services differently.

items.headline: Centre may set up panel to rework UGC equity rules
items.text: On 5 November, the Centre told the Supreme Court it is considering a special committee to re-examine the UGC Equity Regulations 2026. It said the aim is that no group feels excluded or threatened. The rules were notified on 13 January. They require colleges to set up equity committees and handle discrimination complaints. Petitioners from the general category say the rules shut them out. That is because Regulation 3(1)(c) defines caste discrimination as acts against SC, ST and OBC members. In January the Court stayed the rules, calling them, at first look, vague and open to misuse. The Court has urged a review so the rules protect every student. Until then, the 2012 UGC rules apply.
items.background: The UGC, India's university regulator, writes the rules colleges must follow on discrimination complaints.
items.why: These rules decide how complaints of caste discrimination are handled on campuses across India, and who can file them.

items.headline: Shah offers special session on SIR; Delhi officer finds fake deletion forms
items.text: In remarks reported on 5 November, Amit Shah said the government is ready for a special Parliament session on SIR, the Election Commission's revision of voter lists. His condition is that Rahul Gandhi first writes to PM Modi. He dismissed Gandhi's call for a public debate. In Delhi, north-east District Election Officer Ajay Kumar said an independent check found 36 of 37 Form 7 requests in Mustafabad false or fabricated. Form 7 is the form used to ask for a name to be removed from the voter list. His office has filed a police complaint seeking an FIR. Separately, former Chief Election Commissioner S.Y. Quraishi said the West Bengal election was not legally valid.
items.background: Opposition parties are protesting SIR, saying the voter-list revision could wrongly remove voters. The government and opposition have traded challenges over debating it.
items.why: Fake Form 7 requests can remove real voters from the rolls, so this check shows how the revision could be misused.

items.headline: ADNOC signs 10-year gas deal; ONGC seeks control of Venezuelan oilfields
items.text: On 6 November, The Hindu reported that ADNOC had signed a 10-year deal to supply LNG (liquefied natural gas, which is gas cooled into a liquid for shipping) to Gujarat Energy. This would be ADNOC's fifth long-term LNG supply deal with India. Separately, ONGC expects to win operatorship rights in two Venezuelan oil projects within three to six months. Operatorship is the right to run day-to-day work on a field. ONGC holds 40% of the San Cristobal project and 11% of Carabobo. Reuters reported that ONGC hopes to get the rights within six months. The next thing to watch is whether the handover happens by about May 2027.
items.background: ONGC already owns shares in two Venezuelan oil projects. Holding a share is different from operating a field, which means running it day to day.
items.why: Both moves add to India's long-term energy supply from abroad: a decade of gas from ADNOC and more say over Venezuelan oil.

sections.title: Your money & life
sections.gist: Delhi's air nears 'severe' before Diwali on 8 November, and CBSE sets Class 10 exams for 16 February to 9 March 2027.

items.headline: Delhi air nears 'severe' level ahead of Diwali on 8 November
items.text: At 9 am on 6 November, Delhi's overall Air Quality Index (AQI) was 391, rated 'very poor'. The AQI turns air readings into one number; above 400 counts as 'severe'. So Delhi was 9 points short. Half the city's monitors were already there: 30 of 59 stations recorded severe air. The early warning system expects Delhi's first severe day of the season. It expects severe conditions to last until 8 November, Diwali. Firecracker smoke could make it worse. These reports do not say which new restrictions apply. If you are in Delhi, watch the daily AQI and official advisories through Diwali.
items.background: The AQI is a single pollution score. In India, 301–400 is 'very poor' and anything above 400 is 'severe'.
items.why: Millions in Delhi will breathe some of the season's worst air over Diwali, when firecrackers add more smoke.

items.headline: CBSE Class 10 board exams run 16 February to 9 March 2027
items.text: On 6 November, CBSE released the 2027 date sheet for Class 10. Phase 1 of the board exams starts on 16 February and ends on 9 March 2027. That is about three weeks. The main papers: Maths on 17 February, Science on 22 February, English on 26 February and Social Science on 8 March. Most papers run from 10:30 am to 1:30 pm. Some run from 10:30 am to 12:30 pm, depending on the subject. Students now have roughly three months before the first paper. Check the official CBSE website for your exact subject codes and dates.
items.background: CBSE is India's central school board. Its Class 10 exams now follow a two-phase system, and this schedule covers Phase 1.
items.why: Lakhs of families can now plan study time, travel and leave around fixed exam dates.

sections.title: Markets & money
sections.gist: Strong US jobs data points to a December Fed hike, India's forex reserves fall, and China blocks SoftBank's robotics deal.

items.headline: Strong US jobs data points to a December Fed rate rise
items.text: US employers added 165,000 jobs in October, figures released on 6 November showed. Forecasters expected about 65,000, so the real number was roughly 2.5 times higher. Unemployment fell to 4.1%. The Financial Times said the data sets up a rate rise by the Federal Reserve, the US central bank, in December. Here is why. More hiring means more spending. More spending can push prices up. A central bank raises rates to cool that. The Fed held rates at 3.75%–4.00% on 28 October, at chair Kevin Warsh's first meeting. Its December meeting is the next test.
items.background: The Fed raised rates in September, then held them on 28 October at Kevin Warsh's first meeting as chair, in a 10-2 vote.
items.why: Higher US rates usually pull money towards the dollar, which can weaken the rupee and draw investment out of India.

items.headline: Big investors doubt Anthropic's IPO can hit $1.5 trillion
items.text: Major investors doubt that Anthropic's planned stock market listing can value the AI company at $1.5 trillion. The Wall Street Journal reported this in an exclusive published on 6 November. An IPO, or initial public offering, is when a private company first sells shares to the public. Investing.com, citing the Journal, said the pushback follows the recent sell-off in tech stocks. After a sell-off, buyers are often less willing to pay high prices for future growth. It is not yet known whether Anthropic will lower its target or change its timing.
items.background: Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI models, is preparing to list on the stock market at a reported $1.5 trillion target valuation.
items.why: How investors price this IPO is a test of how much money markets will still put into AI after the sell-off.

items.headline: China blocks SoftBank's $5.4 billion purchase of ABB's robotics arm
items.text: China blocked Japanese investor SoftBank's $5.4 billion takeover of the robotics division of ABB, the Swiss-Swedish engineering group. The Financial Times reported the block on 5 November. Large deals often need approval from every major country where the companies do business. That gives each country a veto, and China used its veto here. The New York Times said the move impedes foreign deals in China. The Wall Street Journal said it shows Beijing flexing control over AI technology. It is not yet known whether SoftBank and ABB will restructure the deal or drop it.
items.background: Big cross-border takeovers need approval from regulators in each major market where the companies operate. China is one of them.
items.why: It signals China will use deal approvals to keep control of robotics and AI technology, which affects global companies' plans.

items.headline: India's forex reserves fall $2.69 billion as inflation worries grow
items.text: India's foreign exchange reserves fell by $2.69 billion to $717 billion, data released on 6 November showed. That is a drop of under half a percent. The Hindu reported that experts link it to two things. Money from FCNR(B) deposits was deployed; these are foreign-currency deposits held by Indians living abroad. The RBI also sold dollars to support the rupee. A Reuters poll expects October retail inflation near the top of the RBI's target range, driven by food prices. Higher inflation raises the chance of another rate hike at the RBI's December meeting.
items.background: The RBI raised its repo rate, the rate at which it lends to banks, to 5.5% in October 2026 as inflation rose.
items.why: Another RBI hike would likely make home and car loan EMIs costlier for borrowers in India.

items.headline: SEBI relaxes currency derivative rules; new settlement rules start
items.text: SEBI, India's market regulator, has revised its rules for currency derivatives, Outlook Money reported on 6 November. Currency derivatives are contracts that bet on or protect against moves in exchange rates. Traders may now hold unhedged positions of up to $5 million. 'Unhedged' means the position is not tied to a real currency need, such as paying for imports. Separately, SEBI's new rules for settling administrative and civil cases take effect on 7 November. A settlement lets a person or firm close an enforcement case by paying an agreed amount instead of going through a full proceeding.
items.background: SEBI regulates India's stock and derivatives markets. It can take enforcement action against people or firms that break market rules.
items.why: Traders and companies get more room in currency markets, and anyone facing SEBI action now settles under new rules.

items.headline: Race to replace Lagarde at the ECB moves towards December decision
items.text: Euro area governments faced a deadline on 6 November to nominate candidates to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank (ECB). Eurogroup president Kyriakos Pierrakakis set that deadline. The Eurogroup is the meeting of euro area finance ministers. Bloomberg said the deadline would show whether the contest is a two-horse race. An EU official said leaders aim to appoint the new ECB chief in December. The ECB sets interest rates for the 20-plus countries that use the euro. The final list of candidates is expected once nominations are confirmed.
items.background: The ECB sets interest rates for the countries that use the euro. Christine Lagarde is its current president.
items.why: The next ECB chief will shape euro interest rates, which move global currencies and affect trade with Europe, a major partner for India.

sections.title: Tech & AI
sections.gist: Opposition to AI data centres grows, OpenAI limits a powerful hacking model to vetted users, and METR says AI may double Anthropic's research speed.

items.headline: Anger over AI data centres spreads from Amsterdam to US Congress
items.text: Opposition to AI data centres is growing. On 6 November, protesters broke into a Microsoft data centre being built in Amsterdam. Campaigners plan protests in 16 countries and want a pause on new data centres in Europe. They say the building boom threatens water, power grids and climate goals. In the US, top Democrats called for a national data centre moratorium, a full pause, after their midterm wins. Reuters reported they plan many AI bills once they control Congress. On 5 November, OpenAI pledged to pay all power and grid costs for its data centres. It also dropped secrecy agreements for local councils.
items.background: Data centres are huge buildings of computers that run AI. They use large amounts of electricity and water, which can raise local costs.
items.why: Who pays for AI's power and water is becoming a political fight, and any town hosting data centres faces the same questions.

items.headline: OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber finds 81 Firefox flaws, gets top risk rating
items.text: On 5 November, OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber, an AI model for security work. Only approved customers in its Daybreak Red programme can use it at first. They are allowed to do offensive work, such as writing exploits and 'red teaming', which means attacking systems to test them. Researchers used it to find 81 unknown serious flaws in the Firefox browser. Mozilla has started fixing them. The model also helped build working exploits for 948 Linux kernel flaws. Of these, 588 were previously unknown, about six in ten. OpenAI rated the model 'Critical', its highest cyber-risk level. Wider access is planned over the coming weeks.
items.background: An exploit is code that uses a software flaw to break in. Defenders find flaws to fix them; attackers find them to use them.
items.why: The same tool can protect or attack the software on many computers, so fast patching matters more than ever.

items.headline: Google, Meta and TikTok sue to stop California's child social media law
items.text: On 5 November, Meta, TikTok and Google's parent Alphabet filed three separate federal lawsuits to block a California law, AB 1709. Governor Gavin Newsom signed it in September, and it takes effect on 1 January. The law targets app features it treats as psychologically exploitative for children aged 15 and younger. The companies say it breaks free speech protections and ignores Section 230. Section 230 is a US law that largely shields platforms from liability for what users post. California Attorney General Rob Bonta says he will defend the law. Courts may decide whether to pause it before 1 January.
items.background: Several governments are trying to limit features that keep children scrolling. Tech companies often challenge such laws in court.
items.why: No direct effect in India, but the result will shape how far governments anywhere can regulate apps children use.

items.headline: METR: Anthropic's benchmark progress has roughly doubled since October 2025
items.text: METR, an outside group that reviewed Anthropic, concluded that Anthropic is probably improving its models on well-specified tasks at about twice its rate from March 2024 to October 2025. Its central estimate is that benchmark scores have grown about 1.9 times faster since October 2025. METR's 95% confidence interval runs from 1.5 to 2.8 times faster. This is a range its method treats as very likely to contain the true value. METR's best guess, which it calls subjective, is that about 80% of the speedup comes from Anthropic using AI in its own research. METR is confident that faster growth in computing power is not the cause. The review ran from 12 August to 29 October 2026. Anthropic redacted most of the evidence METR found most informative. METR warns that it may have missed bottlenecks.
items.background: AI companies increasingly use their own AI tools to help build newer models. METR was given access to review this at Anthropic.
items.why: It is an outside attempt to measure whether AI is speeding up the work of building AI itself.

sections.title: Science, health & climate
sections.gist: US measles and bird flu deaths; India rehearses for a foot-and-mouth strain spreading through West Asia; COP31 starts 9 November.

items.headline: Wisconsin infant dies of measles; US records first 2026 bird flu death
items.text: On 5 November, Wisconsin health officials said an infant in the southwest of the state had died of measles, as an outbreak there grows. The coroner listed measles as the cause. It is Wisconsin's first measles death since 1990, 36 years ago. Separately, a resident of Yakima County, Washington, died of H5N1 bird flu after contact with infected dairy cattle. It is the first US bird flu death of 2026. Officials say the risk to the public is low. US Department of Agriculture labs also confirmed H5N1 in a dairy herd in Indiana. It is the state's first case in cattle, and routine national milk testing found it.
items.background: Measles is a highly contagious virus that a vaccine prevents. H5N1 is a bird flu virus that has also been infecting US dairy cattle.
items.why: There is no direct effect in India. The bird flu death shows how a virus in farm animals can reach people.

items.headline: India rehearses response to foot-and-mouth strain spreading through West Asia
items.text: India held a national preparedness exercise called VAJRA-SAT at ICAR-NIVEDI in Bengaluru, the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) said on 6 November. The exercise targets one threat: SAT-1, a strain of foot-and-mouth disease. SAT-1 was traditionally found only in Africa. It has now spread to 17 countries across West Asia. It has not been reported in India. If it did arrive, it would put India's livestock population of over 530 million animals at risk. It would also threaten dairy-based livelihoods and the livestock trade. The aim of the exercise is for India to be ready before any case appears.
items.background: Foot-and-mouth disease is a fast-spreading viral illness of cattle, buffalo, sheep and goats. It comes in several strains, called serotypes.
items.why: Over 530 million animals, plus dairy livelihoods and livestock trade, would be exposed if SAT-1 entered India.

items.headline: COP31 climate summit runs in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 November
items.text: The UN's yearly climate summit, COP31, runs from 9 to 20 November 2026 at the Antalya Expo Center in Türkiye. Two countries share the leadership. Türkiye's environment minister, Murat Kurum, is COP President. Australia's Chris Bowen is President of Negotiations, the role that steers the talks between countries. On 6 November, UN News published an explainer on what is at stake at the summit. The summit is scheduled to close on 20 November. What countries agree, and on which issues, will not be known until then.
items.background: A COP is the yearly UN meeting where countries negotiate how to slow climate change and deal with its effects.
items.why: Agreements made at COPs set the shared global climate rules that India and other countries negotiate and sign up to.

sections.title: Formula 1
sections.gist: Champion Antonelli tops Brazil practice ahead of an upgraded McLaren. Ferrari says the Hamilton–Leclerc air is cleared before the 8 November race.

items.headline: Champion Antonelli fastest in Brazil practice, upgraded McLaren close behind
items.text: Practice for the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos ran on 6 November. Lando Norris topped first practice in a heavily upgraded McLaren. In second practice, Kimi Antonelli, the newly crowned world champion, set the fastest lap: 1 minute 10.763 seconds. That was 0.253 seconds quicker than Norris, about a quarter of a second. Max Verstappen was third. Practice times are only a rough guide, because teams run different fuel loads and car settings. The race is on Sunday, 8 November.
items.background: Antonelli has already won the 2026 drivers' title, so this race is about the win, not the championship.
items.why: It shows whether McLaren's big upgrade has closed the gap to the champion's car.

items.headline: Ferrari boss says air cleared between Hamilton and Leclerc
items.text: Ferrari held crunch talks at Interlagos on 6 November after Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc clashed at the Mexican Grand Prix. Afterwards, Ferrari chief Fred Vasseur said he had cleared the air. He told both drivers they can race hard but must respect each other and the team. Vasseur said Ferrari "failed collectively" in Mexico because it was running first and second and still did not win. On 5 November, Hamilton said Leclerc races him harder than he raced other rivals. He said he would never apologise for his lap-one moves in Mexico. The São Paulo race on 8 November is the first test of the truce.
items.background: Hamilton and Leclerc are team-mates at Ferrari. When team-mates fight on track, the team can lose points both cars could have scored.
items.why: Ferrari ran first and second in Mexico and still lost; how its drivers behave decides its remaining results.

sections.title: Cricket — the masala
sections.gist: Shami retires from Tests with 229 wickets. New Zealand lose Conway to concussion but have Henry cleared for Wellington.

items.headline: Mohammed Shami retires from Test cricket with 229 wickets
items.text: Fast bowler Mohammed Shami, 36, retired from Test cricket on 6 November 2026. That was exactly 13 years after his Test debut against West Indies in 2013. He finishes with 229 wickets from 64 Tests, about three and a half wickets per match. That includes six five-wicket hauls. ESPNcricinfo says he ends as India's sixth-most successful fast bowler in Tests. His last Test was against Australia in June 2023, so India's Test pace attack has already gone more than three years without him. He will keep playing white-ball cricket, the one-day and T20 formats.
items.background: A five-wicket haul means taking five or more wickets in one innings, the usual mark of a match-winning bowling performance.
items.why: It formally closes the Test career of one of India's most successful fast bowlers; he stays available for white-ball cricket.

items.headline: Conway out of India ODI series with concussion; Henry cleared
items.text: New Zealand's Devon Conway has been ruled out of the rest of the one-day international (ODI) series against India. He suffered a concussion during training on 3 November 2026. A player called Kelly has been called into the squad as cover. Matt Henry was also hurt in a training collision. He has been cleared of concussion and is available for the second ODI in Wellington. Concussion rules make a player sit out until doctors clear them. A second blow to a brain that has not healed is dangerous.
items.background: India are in New Zealand for an ODI series, 50 overs per side. The second match is in Wellington.
items.why: New Zealand must change their side mid-series, which shapes the team India face in Wellington.

quiz.q: Chip shares crash worldwide on the same day. Which market is likely to hold up best?
options: One where chip firms make up half the index
One where chip firms are a tenth and bank shares are rising
None: in a global crash every market falls by the same amount
quiz.why: An index moves by each group's weight times its move. A small chip weight plus rising banks can even leave it higher.

quiz.q: Why did correcting Ueno's books push its capital below the legal minimum?
options: Expenses wrongly counted as assets were removed, shrinking the cushion
Depositors withdrew their money too quickly
The central bank suddenly raised the legal minimum
quiz.why: Capital is assets minus what the bank owes. Removing fake assets shrinks capital directly, before any money leaves the bank.

quiz.q: Why does a Democratic Congress make Trump's choice of chief of staff matter more?
options: The chief of staff can overrule votes in Congress
With new laws harder to pass, more governing runs through White House staff and executive action
The Senate must now approve the chief of staff
quiz.why: Blocked in Congress, a president leans on executive powers. The chief of staff runs that machine and needs no Senate approval.
